item.title: 2-of-3 Multisig Explained: How It Works and What It Costs
item.description: How 2-of-3 bitcoin multisig works, what each pair of keys is for, how it compares with single-sig, and the real costs: fees, backups and complexity.
item.content:encoded:
A 2-of-3 multisig wallet holds bitcoin behind three keys and lets any two of them spend. Lose one key and the other two still move your money. Have one key stolen and the thief still cannot spend. That is the whole idea, and it is enforced by Bitcoin itself, not by a company or an app. This article explains how it works under the hood, what each pair of keys is good for, how it compares with an ordinary single-key wallet, and what it costs you in fees, backups and care.

What "2-of-3" means

A normal bitcoin wallet has one private key (in practice, one seed phrase that produces many keys). Whoever holds that seed can spend. This is called single-sig: one signature is enough.

A multisig wallet replaces that single key with a rule: M signatures out of N possible keys. In a 2-of-3 wallet there are three keys, usually kept on three different devices or in three different places, and any two of them must sign before coins can move. The three keys are equal: no key is "the main one" as far as Bitcoin is concerned.

The rule is part of the coins themselves. When you receive bitcoin to a multisig address, the address commits to a script that says "two valid signatures from these three public keys". Every node on the network checks that rule before accepting a spend. No server can waive it, and no single key can break it.

How a 2-of-3 wallet works under the hood

You do not need these details to use multisig, but they explain the backup advice later on.

Three extended public keys

Each of the three devices holds its own seed and exports an extended public key (an xpub) for a multisig account. A common standard for the account path is BIP 48, for example m/48'/0'/0'/2' for a native segwit multisig account on mainnet. The xpub lets the wallet derive public keys but not spend.

One address per index, from all three keys

For each new receive address, the wallet takes the next public key from each of the three xpubs and builds a script that requires two signatures from those three keys. Today that script is usually wrapped as a P2WSH (native segwit) output, so the address starts with bc1q and is longer than a single-sig one.

The descriptor ties it together

The full recipe for the wallet, "2 of these three xpubs, at these paths, in a P2WSH script", is written as an output descriptor. For a 2-of-3 it looks like this (shortened):

wsh(sortedmulti(2,[f00d1234/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6E.../0/*,[ab12cd34/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6F.../0/*,[99887766/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6D.../0/*))

wsh is the P2WSH wrapper, sortedmulti(2, …) means "two of these keys, sorted into a fixed order", and each bracket names the device fingerprint and path a key came from. Descriptors are standardised in BIP 380 and BIP 383, and Bitcoin Core documents them in its descriptors guide. The descriptor holds no secret, but it is essential: without the other keys' xpubs, your seed alone cannot find your coins.

Signing passes a PSBT around

To spend, one device creates a Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction (BIP 174), signs it, and hands it to a second device, which adds its signature. Once two signatures are in, the transaction is complete and can be broadcast. The PSBT can travel over USB, Bluetooth, a QR code, an SD card or a network message; the signatures are what matter.

What each pair of keys is for

Because any two keys spend, a 2-of-3 setup gives you three different pairs. Good designs give each pair a job:

  • Everyday pair. Two keys that are easy to reach together, for routine spending.
  • Big-decision pair. A pair that includes a key kept offline, for large payments or for changing how the wallet behaves.
  • Recovery pair. The two keys you still have when one is lost or stolen. They move everything to a new wallet with a fresh third key.

The important property: no single key can spend, and no single loss locks you out. Both of those are true at the same time, which a single-key wallet cannot offer.

Single-sig vs 2-of-3: what you are trading

People ask whether multisig is "worth it". The honest answer is that it changes which risks you carry rather than removing risk.

Single-sig (one seed)2-of-3 multisig
One key lostFunds lost unless the seed backup existsStill spendable with the other two
One key stolen or seed photographedThief can spend everythingThief cannot spend alone
Backups to keepOne seed (plus passphrase, if used)Each key's backup plus the descriptor
Transaction size and feesSmallestLarger inputs: two signatures and the script
On-chain privacyLooks like most walletsA spend reveals a 2-of-3 script
Setup and recovery effortLowHigher: registration, address checks, more steps

A single seed is a single point of failure in both directions: it can be lost, and it can be found. Adding a BIP 39 passphrase spreads that risk across two items, but whoever learns both still holds a complete key, and losing the passphrase loses the funds.

Multisig removes the single point of failure but adds moving parts. If you store two of the three keys in the same drawer, you are back to one point of failure, with more complexity. If you lose the descriptor and one key, recovery can become very hard.

For a small amount you spend often, a well-backed-up single-sig wallet is a reasonable choice. As the amount grows, or if theft or a single mistake worries you more than complexity does, 2-of-3 starts to pay for itself.

What multisig does not fix

  • Two keys in one place. A burglar who finds two keys in the same house holds a spending pair.
  • Coercion. If someone can force you to use two keys, multisig alone does not stop them. Waiting periods and limits help more here (see Delay & Notify: why recovery should wait).
  • Signing the wrong thing. If malware swaps the destination address and you approve it on both devices without reading the screen, the payment goes out. Devices that show the address you are paying, and the wallet's own change, are what protect you (see choosing a hardware wallet for multisig).
  • Lost metadata. Without the descriptor (or all the xpubs), the keys you hold may not be enough to find the coins.

2-of-3 or 3-of-5?

Larger setups such as 3-of-5 tolerate two lost keys and make theft harder, but every payment needs three devices and every recovery more coordination. For an individual, 2-of-3 is the common middle ground: one loss is survivable, one theft is harmless, and only two devices are needed to sign.

How Trikey approaches it

Trikey is an open-source 2-of-3 wallet in which you hold all three keys, and each pair has one job:

  • Key 1, any hardware wallet (Ledger, Trezor, Coldcard, Jade, BitBox02 and others), kept in a drawer.
  • Key 2, your phone, behind its biometrics.
  • Key 3, the Trikey Guardian, an app on your own home server (Umbrel, Start9 or plain Docker).

Phone plus guardian is the everyday pair: the guardian co-signs phone payments only within a daily limit you set. Phone plus hardware wallet is the big-decision pair: larger payments and any loosening of the rules. Hardware wallet plus guardian is the recovery pair for a lost phone, behind a waiting period with daily alerts.

Under the hood every Trikey wallet is a plain wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) descriptor on BIP 48 paths, the same kind of script shown above. That choice is deliberate: it is the multisig script every major hardware wallet can co-sign, and it means any multisig-capable wallet can recover the coins with two of your keys, without Trikey. The reasons, and what was left out (taproot multisig, miniscript, MuSig2), are in the design document's decisions.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet anyway, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide explains how to try it.

FAQ

Is 2-of-3 multisig safer than a single hardware wallet?

It removes the single point of failure: one lost or stolen key no longer decides the outcome. It is only safer if you keep the three keys apart and back up the descriptor. Done carelessly, it adds ways to make mistakes.

Can I recover a multisig wallet with just the seed words?

Usually not with two seeds alone. You also need the third key's xpub, which is in the descriptor. Keep a copy of the descriptor with each key backup; it reveals your balance and history to whoever reads it, but it cannot spend. More in bitcoin inheritance without a company.

Does multisig cost more in fees?

Yes. Each multisig input carries two signatures and the script, so it is larger than a single-sig input and costs more to spend. Fewer, larger coins keep the difference small.

Can I mix hardware wallet brands in one multisig?

Yes, and many people do, so that one vendor's bug does not affect every key. Each device must support the script type and, ideally, let you register the wallet and check addresses on its screen.

How is multisig different from splitting a seed (Shamir or SLIP-39)?

A split seed is still one key: the shares are combined into the full seed when you need it, at which point it exists in one place. Multisig keeps the keys separate forever; each device signs on its own and no device ever holds the others' keys.

item.title: worse_query: What an iOS Bug Can Take From Your Wallet
item.description: An iOS bug lets malicious apps read other apps' files. What that exposes in a bitcoin wallet, what it doesn't, and what to do today.
item.content:encoded:
On 10 November 2026, Binance warned iPhone users about worse_query, a bug in iOS that lets a malicious app read files that belong to other apps. Binance named seed phrases, private keys and login credentials as being at risk "across the entire ecosystem" (Bitcoin Magazine). That is alarming for anyone with a wallet on their phone. But what a bug like this can take depends on one thing: where your wallet keeps its keys. This post explains that, so you can judge your own wallet, and lists what to do today.

What worse_query is, as reported so far

These are the facts as reported on 10 November 2026. Check the latest news before you act on them.

  • It is a sandbox escape. Every iPhone app is meant to live in its own sandbox: it can read its own files and nobody else's. worse_query breaks that wall, so an app you install can read files that another app wrote.
  • A researcher, forcequitOS, published it as a public proof of concept on 8 November. The security firm SlowMist lists iOS 26.0 to 26.7.2 and iOS 27.2 as affected; Binance's warning names 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2 (SlowMist on X, CryptoTicker). If your version sits between those, assume it is affected too.
  • Apple released iOS 27.2.1 and 26.7.3 on 9 November. SlowMist says 27.2.1 stops the bug, but Apple's security notes don't mention it, so treat the fix as likely, not confirmed (Security Affairs).
  • No attack or theft had been reported when this was written.
  • SlowMist's point is the one that matters here: the bug alone doesn't steal anything. The risk is an untrusted app on your phone, combined with a wallet that keeps seeds, keystores or caches in plain files.
  • The attacker needs an app on your phone. It is not a remote attack: someone has to get you to install a malicious app, most likely from outside the App Store (a "sideloaded" or manually signed app).

Files and the Keychain are two different places

A phone wallet can keep its secrets in two kinds of storage, and worse_query reaches only one of them.

  1. The app's own files. A database, settings, caches. These live in the app's folder, and the sandbox is the only thing that protects them from other apps. A sandbox escape like worse_query reads them.
  2. The Keychain (on Android, the Keystore). It is a system service, not a file in the app's folder. Its items are encrypted with keys guarded by the phone's secure chip (the Secure Enclave on iPhone). An item can also be set to need Face ID or a fingerprint every time it is read, and to never leave the device. A bug that only reads files doesn't hand over what is in the Keychain.

So the question for any wallet is: does it write the seed, or a private key, into its own files? A wallet that keeps them in the Keychain loses privacy to a bug like this: your addresses, your balance, your history. A wallet that keeps a seed in a file, even "obfuscated", can lose the money.

How to find out for your wallet:

  • Look for a security page or a threat model in the wallet's documentation that says where keys are stored. For an open-source wallet you can also read the code.
  • Words to look for: Keychain, Secure Enclave, Android Keystore, "this device only", "biometric".
  • Be wary of wallets that never say. "Bank-grade encryption" doesn't tell you where the key is.

What a file-reading bug can expose

Even when the keys are safe, an app's files hold things you'd rather keep to yourself:

  • Your public keys and addresses. Many wallets store an extended public key (xpub) or a descriptor. With it, someone can list every address of the wallet, so your balance and your whole history. They can't spend with it, but it tells them what you hold, which matters for phishing and physical safety.
  • Labels and notes: what you called each payment and who you paid.
  • Session tokens for exchanges and other services, if an app keeps them in files. This is where "logins at risk" comes from.

What to do today

  1. Update iOS. Settings, General, Software Update. Take the newest version offered: 27.2.1 or later on iOS 27, 26.7.3 or later if your phone stays on iOS 26. On 27.1, 27.0.x or an older 26.x, update.

  2. Remove apps you don't trust, especially ones that didn't come from the App Store: sideloaded or manually signed apps from strangers, "modded" apps, cracked games. The bug needs one of those on your phone to do anything.

  3. Don't panic-move your coins into something new. Scammers follow security news: expect fake "migration tools", fake support accounts and "verify your wallet" messages. Nobody legitimate will ask for your seed words.

  4. If you have reason to think your phone was compromised (a strange app you installed, signs of tampering), treat its keys as exposed:

    • Create a new wallet on a clean, updated device.
    • Move the funds there.
    • Reset your exchange sessions and passwords.

    A restore of the same seed on a new phone isn't enough: whoever has a copy can still use it. Our post on losing a phone, a hardware wallet or a seed phrase goes through the cases.

Why a phone key shouldn't be the only key

worse_query is one bug. There will be others, in iOS, in Android, in apps. That is the strongest argument against keeping all your bitcoin behind one key on a phone. A phone runs hundreds of other apps and connects to everything; it is the most exposed device you own.

With 2-of-3 multisig, the phone's key is one of three, and moving money needs two. A phone bug, even one that did reach the key, would give an attacker one key. Pair that with a daily limit and an alert on the second key, and the worst case of a phone compromise becomes "at most one day's limit", not "everything".

Trikey and worse_query

Trikey is an open-source 2-of-3 wallet: your hardware wallet (key 1), your phone (key 2) and the Trikey Guardian on your own home server (key 3). How it stands against a file-reading bug:

  • Key 2 lives in the Keychain, set to "this device only", never in backups, and readable only with Face ID. Every other key the app holds is in the Keychain or Keystore too. The app's files hold the wallet's public descriptor, the guardian's pairing details, labels and history: a privacy loss if read, with no power to sign. The full list, item by item, is in what the phone app keeps, and where.
  • Even key 2 alone moves at most the daily limit. The guardian co-signs phone-only payments within a limit you set. Raising the limit, changing a rule or starting a recovery needs your hardware wallet, or waits through a Delay & Notify period that alerts you every day (rules the guardian enforces).
  • If you suspect your phone, you can lock the guardian from the phone or its web page, restore key 2 on a clean phone from your backup, and use "Replace guardian" to move your coins to a fresh wallet.
  • About "manually signed apps": while the iPhone app isn't on the App Store, testers build Trikey themselves from its public source code, which iOS counts as a manually signed app. Building an open-source app yourself is not what the warning is about. The warning is about apps from people you don't know. Keep your own build, update iOS, and remove anything you don't trust.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet anyway, use only an amount you can afford to lose.

FAQ

Is my seed phrase exposed by worse_query?

Only if your wallet writes it into its own files. Wallets that keep the seed in the iPhone Keychain, especially with Face ID required, are not exposed by a bug that only reads files. Check your wallet's documentation, update iOS, and remove apps you don't trust.

Do I need to move my bitcoin?

Not because of the news alone. Move it if you installed something you don't trust, or see signs your phone was tampered with. Then move it to a wallet created on a clean device, not to the same seed restored elsewhere.

Does a hardware wallet protect me?

Its keys never touch the phone, so a phone bug can't read them. What it can reveal is your xpub, if a companion app stores it: that is privacy, not access to the coins.

item.title: Lost Your Hardware Wallet, Phone or Seed Phrase?
item.description: What happens to your bitcoin if you lose a hardware wallet, a phone or a seed phrase, case by case, with the steps to take and the scams to avoid.
item.content:encoded:
Your bitcoin is not inside your hardware wallet or your phone. It sits on the blockchain, locked to keys, and a device is only a safe place to keep and use those keys. So what losing a device means depends on one question: do you still have another way to produce the same keys? This guide goes through the common cases, from a lost device with a good backup to a lost seed phrase, for single-key wallets and for multisig, and says what to do in each.

First, three rules that apply to every case

  1. Nobody can recover keys for you. No support desk, "recovery service" or website can bring back a lost seed phrase. People who search for help after a loss are a favourite target for scams: fake support numbers, paid "recovery" firms and pages that ask you to type your seed words. Never enter seed words on a website or give them to anyone.
  2. If a key may be in someone else's hands, move the coins. A backup lets you restore, but it does not make the lost copy harmless. When in doubt, send everything to a new wallet with fresh keys.
  3. Act on the backup you actually have. Check it before you need it: the words are legible, the order is right, and any passphrase is recorded somewhere you will find it.

Single-key wallets: case by case

You lost the hardware wallet but have the seed phrase

Your funds are safe. Restore the seed phrase on a new device (same brand or any other that supports the standard, usually BIP 39), add the passphrase if you used one, and check that your balance appears.

Then decide whether to move the coins. The lost device is protected by its PIN, and most devices wipe or permanently lock themselves after a number of wrong PINs, but you cannot know who has it or what they can try. If the amount matters, create a new wallet with a new seed, back it up, and send everything to it.

The device was stolen

Same steps, with more urgency. Restore from your seed on another device and move the funds to a fresh wallet before a thief has time to work on the PIN or the device.

You still have the device but lost the seed phrase

Nothing is lost yet, but you are one accident away from it. Do not wait:

  1. Set up a new wallet with a new seed and write that seed down carefully.
  2. Check the new backup (many devices offer a "verify backup" step).
  3. Send all funds from the old wallet to the new one.

Avoid trying to "recover" the old seed through software or online tools. A new, properly backed-up wallet is faster and safer.

Your seed phrase may have been seen

A photo in the cloud, a sheet left in a drawer that someone else opened, words typed into a website: treat the seed as compromised. Move everything to a new wallet with a new seed now. Restoring or "securing" the old seed does nothing.

You lost both the device and the seed phrase

If there is no other copy of the seed and no wallet file on an old computer, the coins cannot be moved by anyone. This is the hard edge of self-custody, and the main reason people move to setups with more than one key.

A phone wallet was lost or stolen

For a single-key wallet on a phone, the seed phrase backup is everything. If you have it, restore it on another device and move the funds to a new wallet: the old phone still holds a copy of the key, protected only by its screen lock and the app's own lock. Also lock or erase the phone remotely and secure the email and phone number accounts it was signed into.

Multisig wallets: losing one key is survivable

In a 2-of-3 multisig wallet any two keys spend, so losing one key is an inconvenience, not a loss.

The recovery routine

  1. Use the two keys you still have.
  2. Create a new wallet: the two surviving keys plus a fresh third key (often at a new account on the same devices).
  3. Send everything from the old wallet to the new one.
  4. Back up the new wallet's descriptor and the new key.

Why move instead of just replacing the lost device? The old wallet's rule includes the lost key forever. If someone finds that key, they hold one of the three. Moving to a new wallet takes it out of the picture.

What you need besides the keys

Two seeds alone are usually not enough to find the coins. Your wallet software also needs the descriptor: the three public keys and how they are combined. Keep a copy of it with each key backup. It holds no secret (it cannot spend), but it shows your balance and history to whoever reads it.

When two keys are lost

If two of three keys are gone, a 2-of-3 wallet is in the same position as a single-key wallet with no backup. Restore whatever seeds you have from their backups before you consider anything else.

Why some wallets make you wait

Some wallets let a single surviving key start a recovery, but only after a waiting period, with alerts sent to you during it. The point is to make a stolen key slow and noisy rather than fast and silent: if you did not start the recovery, you have days to cancel it. We cover this in Delay & Notify: why recovery should wait.

How Trikey approaches it

Trikey is a 2-of-3 wallet with a hardware wallet (key 1), your phone (key 2) and the Trikey Guardian on your own home server (key 3). Its recovery flows follow the cases above:

What you lostWhat happens in Trikey
Phone, with its backupRestore the phone key on a new phone from your encrypted backup file and recovery code. No waiting.
Phone, no backupThe hardware wallet lets a new phone reach the guardian, and a recovery starts. It waits 7, 14 or 30 days (your choice), alerts you and your alert contacts every day, and any of you can cancel it. Then the money moves to a new 2-of-3 wallet.
Phone stolenA thief with an unlocked phone can spend at most your daily limit. Raising the limit needs the hardware wallet. Starting a recovery pauses phone-only payments.
Hardware walletRestore its seed words on a new device, or use the phone and guardian to run the same waiting-period recovery.
Hardware wallet stolenIt is PIN-locked and one key of three. A recovery someone starts with it triggers the daily alerts, and you cancel it.
Home server dies or is stolenThe phone and hardware wallet still move any amount. "Replace guardian" moves the coins to a new wallet with a new guardian. The guardian keeps key 3 encrypted and locks itself after any restart, so an unplugged box is useless to a thief.

Because the wallet is a standard wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) descriptor, any two of your keys can also move the coins in another multisig wallet, without Trikey.

The full table, including the cases where a thief and the owner each hold one key, is in the design document's recovery flows and threat model. The site's pick a key to lose section walks through it with short videos.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide includes a step where you delete the app and restore from your backup, which is worth rehearsing with any wallet.

FAQ

Is my bitcoin gone if I lose my hardware wallet?

No, not if you have the seed phrase (and passphrase, if you used one). Restore it on a new device. Consider moving the funds to a fresh wallet afterwards.

Can the manufacturer recover my wallet?

No. Hardware wallet makers do not have your seed. Anyone claiming to recover a wallet for a fee, or asking for your seed words, should be treated as a scam.

I forgot my PIN but have the seed. What now?

Most devices wipe or lock themselves after too many wrong attempts, and many let you reset them. Either way, restore from the seed phrase on the reset device or a new one.

Should I move my coins after restoring?

If the lost device or seed could be in someone else's hands, yes. A restore gives you access; only a move to new keys makes the lost copy worthless.

What do I need to recover a multisig wallet?

Enough keys to meet the threshold (two of three for 2-of-3) and the wallet's descriptor. With both, any multisig-capable wallet can rebuild it.
